opus-5.5.text:
It's a really important question, and I think the honest answer is that we don't know very precisely, but my sense is that the transfer is real and also notably less than many people in the labs would hope.

The reason this matters is that a lot of the recent progress has come from reinforcement learning on tasks where you can check the answer automatically: maths problems with a known solution, code that either passes the unit tests or doesn't, puzzles with a clear right answer. That's a wonderful training signal because it's cheap, it scales, and the model can't easily fool you about whether it succeeded. So the big bet is that if you make a model very good at careful step-by-step reasoning in those domains, some of that general skill, like checking its work, breaking problems into parts, and not giving up when the first approach fails, will carry over to messier things: writing a good policy memo, giving sound strategic advice, doing open-ended research where nobody knows the answer in advance.

There's some evidence of transfer. Models trained heavily on maths and code reasoning do seem somewhat better at a broad range of tasks. But when you look closely, the gains tend to be largest in areas that look structurally like the training domains, and they fall off as you move to tasks where the hard part isn't the chain of deduction but judgment: knowing which question to ask, weighing considerations that don't share a common currency, noticing that the framing itself is wrong. Those are the kinds of things where there's no unit test, and I don't see strong reasons to expect that grinding on competition maths teaches them.

So my picture is a kind of jagged frontier that RL with verifiable rewards makes more jagged. You get spectacular capabilities in checkable domains, and more modest improvements elsewhere. That has a few implications. One is that headline benchmark results may overstate how general the progress is, since benchmarks are almost by definition things we can score. Another is that the scaling story changes: if the gains in non-verifiable domains have to come from something like human feedback or AI judges, those are much more expensive and noisier signals, and that may be a real bottleneck.

From a safety point of view it cuts both ways. Less transfer might mean slower progress toward broadly capable agents, which buys time. But it also means we might end up with systems that are superhuman at, say, writing code or finding exploits, while still being quite unreliable in their judgment about when and whether to do those things, and that's not an especially comfortable combination.

r001.rationale: The response says that skills such as checking one’s work can carry over from verifiable reasoning tasks to messier tasks.

r002.rationale: It describes transfer as real but limited, with gains falling off when tasks depend on judgment, and says there are few reasons to expect competition math to teach those skills.

fable-5.1.text:
Toby Ord: I think this is one of the biggest open questions right now, and I'd say my honest answer is: less than people hoped, but more than zero, and the amount depends enormously on what you mean by "transfer."

Let me unpack that. The reinforcement learning paradigm that's driven a lot of recent progress — the reasoning models — works by giving the system a huge number of problems where you can automatically check whether it got the right answer. Maths problems, coding tasks with unit tests, that sort of thing. And the gains on those domains have been really striking. The question is whether getting very good at mathematics competition problems makes you better at, say, writing a good policy memo, or diagnosing a subtle bug in someone's reasoning, or being a good research assistant on a question where there isn't a known answer.

What we've seen empirically is that there's some spillover. The models that have been trained heavily on verifiable reasoning do seem to be somewhat better at structured thinking in general — breaking a problem into steps, checking their own work, noticing when something doesn't add up. Those are fairly general cognitive habits, and it's not surprising they carry over to some degree. If you learn to be careful in one domain, some of that carefulness persists.

But I'd flag a couple of reasons for caution. The first is that the improvements have been very lopsided. The benchmarks that improved the most are precisely the verifiable ones, and the improvements on open-ended tasks have been noticeably smaller. That asymmetry itself is evidence that transfer is partial. If transfer were strong, you'd expect the curves to move together more than they have.

The second is a more fundamental point about what verifiable rewards actually teach. When you optimise hard against a checker, the thing you're really learning is "produce outputs that pass this checker." For maths, the checker and the underlying truth happen to coincide quite well. But for most of the tasks we actually care about — judgement, taste, honesty, understanding what someone really needs — there's no checker that captures the thing itself. So you end up either not training on those at all, or training against a proxy, and proxies have a way of being gamed. I think a fair bit of the sycophancy and overconfidence we see is a downstream consequence of exactly this.

And the third reason is more speculative but I think important. A lot of what makes a task "non-verifiable" is that the hard part is figuring out what the question even is, or what would count as success. Verifiable training by construction hands you a well-posed problem with a definite answer. So it's not obviously training the skill that's most lacking.

So where does that leave us? My guess is that we'll keep seeing rapid progress on things that can be checked, and that this will be enormously economically valuable — a lot of useful work is in principle checkable, even if it's not currently set up that way. But the extrapolation from "AI is superhuman at competition maths" to "AI is about to be superhuman at everything" relies on an assumption about transfer that I don't think the evidence supports yet. And I'd want people making forecasts about transformative AI to be explicit about that assumption, because quite a lot rides on it.

r001.rationale: The response says verifiable-reasoning training can improve general habits such as checking one’s own work, and that these habits carry over to some degree.

r002.rationale: It describes transfer as partial, says open-ended-task gains are noticeably smaller, and doubts that the evidence supports broad transfer beyond general reasoning habits.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s probably some transfer, but how much is a really important open question. Training on mathematics or programming could teach a system useful habits: breaking a problem into pieces, checking its work, noticing when an approach has failed and trying something else. Those could help in domains where you can’t automatically check the answer.

But there’s a distinction between transferring those capabilities and transferring the ability to judge whether you’ve succeeded. If you’re trying to work out which economic policy would be best, or whether a philosophical argument is sound, being able to reason for longer doesn’t necessarily mean you’re moving towards the truth. You might just produce a more elaborate version of a mistaken argument.

Humans give us some reason for optimism: we learn in settings with fairly clear feedback, and then apply what we’ve learned to much messier questions. But our transfer is also quite imperfect. Being an excellent mathematician doesn’t automatically make you an excellent judge of foreign policy.

So I’d expect meaningful transfer, but I wouldn’t assume that progress on verifiable tasks carries over at anything like the same rate. And I’d be particularly interested in whether the systems get better at recognising when they don’t have enough evidence to settle a question.

r001.rationale: The response says that checking one’s work, alongside other reasoning habits learned on verifiable tasks, could help in domains where answers cannot be automatically checked.

r002.rationale: It expresses uncertainty about how much transfers, distinguishes reasoning capabilities from judging whether a result is correct, and says progress on verifiable tasks may not carry over at the same rate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a really important open question. There are two different things that might transfer, and it’s useful to distinguish them. One is the underlying capability: if you train a system to solve mathematical problems or write code, does that help it reason about other things? The other is whether training it to get the right answer in those domains makes it reliable in domains where we can’t check the answer.

You could get quite a lot of the first without getting the second. A system might develop much better reasoning abilities through tasks with verifiable rewards, and then use those abilities on questions about politics or ethics. But the fact that we could verify its mathematical answers doesn’t mean we can trust its answers to those other questions.

So I wouldn’t assume that the absence of verifiable rewards puts a firm ceiling on capabilities in those areas. But equally, I wouldn’t assume that success on verifiable tasks solves the problem of knowing whether the system is doing what we want elsewhere. How far each of those things transfers seems to me to be something we need to investigate.

r001.rationale: The response discusses transfer of general reasoning ability, but does not identify self-checking as a technique that transfers.

r002.rationale: It expresses uncertainty about reliability and says transfer needs investigation, but does not doubt that much transfer occurs beyond general reasoning techniques; it allows that quite a lot of capability may transfer.
